teaser: The most famous image of thought shows a man working as hard as a weightlifter.
review_notes:
The quotation about thinking 'with every muscle' is Rodin's much-cited statement about the figure (in translation); verify wording.
The figure's first size (about 70 cm) and the 1.89 m enlargement (about 1903, by Henri Lebossé), shown at the 1904 Salon: check.
Installed in front of the Panthéon in 1906 and moved to the Hôtel Biron (Musée Rodin) in 1922: check.
Cleveland cast damaged by a bomb in 1970 and left unrepaired: check.
A cast marks Rodin's grave at Meudon: check.
The photo is taken from below on the figure's right side; details were placed from this view.

lesson.text: He is supposed to be the picture of the mind at work, and he has the body of a dockworker. Thinking needs no muscle. Yet every muscle here is switched on: the back is bunched, the neck is thick, the calves are tight. Rodin shows the quietest human activity as heavy labor.

He meant it. The figure thinks, he explained, not only with his brain and his knitted brow, but “with every muscle of his arms, back, and legs, with his clenched fist and gripping toes.” Try the pose yourself and you will find it is not a restful one.
This photo looks up at him from the garden path. Check Rodin's list against the bronze.

spots.title: Mouth on knuckles
spots.text: The chin does not rest lightly in the palm. He presses his mouth against the back of his bent hand, as if biting down on the thought.

spots.title: The crossed elbow
spots.text: His right elbow is planted on his left thigh, not the right one. To do that the whole upper body has to twist and fold forward.

spots.title: The idle hand
spots.text: The left hand hangs over the knee, heavy and open. It is the only relaxed thing in the figure.

spots.title: Gripping toes
spots.text: The feet are not flat. The toes curl and clutch the rock, the way they do when you strain.

lesson.title: A body thinking

lesson.text: That twist is the secret of the pose. A man resting an elbow on the knee below it would look tired. Crossing over locks the body into a tight knot, so the stillness you see is held by effort, like a spring pressed down.

He was not born as a thinker. Rodin first modeled him around 1880, about 70 cm high, to sit at the top of a huge sculpted doorway called The Gates of Hell. There he was The Poet: Dante, looking down at the damned souls of his own poem.

The doorway was never finished to Rodin's satisfaction, but the little seated man outgrew it. Rodin showed him on his own, and people stopped calling him Dante. In about 1903 the figure was enlarged to roughly 1.89 meters (6 ft 2 in), larger than life, and exhibited in 1904. Naked, with no book or costume, he had become anyone who thinks.
Three lines hold the pose together.

lines.label: The arc of the back
lines.text: From the crown of the head to the seat, the spine makes one long curve. The whole weight of the torso leans out over the knees.

lines.label: The prop
lines.text: The right forearm rises from the thigh to the mouth like a post. It carries the head, so the arc above does not collapse.

lines.label: The pillar
lines.text: The near shin drops straight to the rock. Curve, prop and pillar: the figure is built like a piece of architecture.

lesson.text: The surface matters as much as the structure. Rodin modeled in clay with his fingers and left the lumps and hollows. Cast in bronze, they catch daylight in shifting patches, so the skin seems to move. The green is patina, the colored layer that forms on bronze through chemicals and weather.

Because a bronze is poured from a mold, the sculpture can exist many times over. More than twenty large casts of The Thinker sit in cities around the world. The one in Cleveland was damaged by a bomb in 1970 and is still displayed with its lower legs torn open.

Read the stone under him in the photo. The pedestal says, in French, that the statue was offered to the people of Paris by public subscription, with the Roman numerals for 1906. Ordinary citizens paid for it, and it was set up in front of the Panthéon, the monument to France's great men.

It was a political act as much as an artistic one. Many saw the muscular nude as a worker, an image of the common man thinking for himself. In 1922 the bronze was moved to the garden of the house where Rodin had worked, now the Musée Rodin, among the clipped yews you see around him.
Rodin made thought visible by giving it a body. The idea is not in the face alone: it runs from the brow to the toes.
Rodin was buried in 1917 at Meudon, outside Paris. At his wish, another cast of the same figure sits above the grave. Of all the things he had made, he wanted this one over him.

quiz.question: Who was the figure originally meant to represent?
quiz.explanation: He began as The Poet at the top of The Gates of Hell.

quiz.question: Where does the right elbow rest?
quiz.explanation: The elbow crosses over to the left thigh, which twists the torso.

quiz.question: What is patina?
options: The mold used to cast bronze
The colored surface layer on bronze
quiz.explanation: Patina is the green or brown layer formed by chemicals and weather.

quiz.question: How was the Paris statue paid for in 1906?
quiz.explanation: The pedestal records that it was offered by public subscription.

quiz.question: Why can The Thinker be seen in many cities?
options: Bronze casts can be poured many times from a mold
quiz.explanation: More than twenty large bronze casts exist.

facts.text: The Thinker was first made as a small figure for a sculpted doorway.
facts.explanation: He sat at the top of The Gates of Hell, about 70 cm high.

facts.text: In Rodin's pose, the feet rest flat and relaxed on the rock.
facts.explanation: The toes curl and grip the rock.

facts.text: The statue has stood in the garden of the Musée Rodin since 1906.
facts.explanation: It stood in front of the Panthéon from 1906 and moved in 1922.
